title: Why Difficult Students Need Your Unconditional Acceptance nal-acceptance/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin explores the tension between holding difficult students accountable everywhere on campus and the psychological toll of being constantly scrutinized, which he terms 'the curse of performancism.' He argues that while consistent, campus-wide accountability is non-negotiable, teachers must avoid piling on personal disappointment, lectures, or sarcasm each time a difficult student slips up—since these students already feel their every move is watched and judged. Following the classroom management plan alone is sufficient to communicate that a mistake was made; what these students additionally need is reassurance that misbehavior doesn't define who they are. He concludes that unconditional acceptance—paired with unwavering accountability—releases the pressure of performancism and unlocks students' determination to belong.
points: Teachers must hold students accountable for misbehavior even outside the classroom, but this creates constant scrutiny for difficult students.
'Performancism'—the burden of being constantly watched and judged—can cause difficult students to give up, rebel, or believe misbehavior is 'the only thing they're good at.'
Simply following the classroom management plan consistently is enough to communicate accountability; adding lectures or sarcasm only piles on disappointment.
Difficult students most need reassurance that their mistakes don't define them and that the teacher remains 'in her corner' regardless.
Unconditional acceptance combined with consistent accountability, rather than either alone, is what unlocks lasting behavior change.
quotes: Effective classroom management requires you to hold difficult students accountable beyond just the four walls of your classroom.
Everyone on campus knows who they are and are quick to point out their transgressions.
Thinking too much, too often, and too critically about one's performance can cause unrelenting stress and anxiety. It causes athletes to freeze up, salespeople to fumble their presentations.
Simply following your classroom management plan is enough for her to understand that she made a mistake.
She needs to know that her mistakes don’t define her and that even if she were to mess up every single day, you would still be in her corner and on her side.
Your most difficult students need not your red-faced lectures or your bitter disappointment, but your forgiveness, your grace, and your unconditional acceptance.
